## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ghaṭikāra Sutta* (MN 81) opens when the Buddha smiles while walking in Kosala, prompting Ānanda to ask the reason for his smile [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Galasek 2016]. The Buddha explains that the location was once the dwelling place of the past Buddha Kassapa (Kāśyapa) and narrates a past-life tale concerning two friends: the pious potter Ghaṭikāra—Kassapa Buddha's chief supporter—and the young Brahmin Jotipāla [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Chen 2015]. Ghaṭikāra repeatedly urges Jotipāla to visit Kassapa Buddha, but Jotipāla refuses and makes derogatory remarks about the Buddha before finally being persuaded to go [Anālayo 2013; Chen 2015]. Upon hearing the Dhamma, Jotipāla gains faith and goes forth as a monk under Kassapa [Anālayo 2013; Chen 2015]. At the close of the discourse, the Buddha identifies himself as the former Brahmin youth Jotipāla (*aham tena samayena Jotipālo māṇavo ahosiṃ*), technically rendering the narrative a Jātaka [Norman 1983].

The sutta is considered significant for tracing the emergence and evolution of the bodhisattva doctrine [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2013]. Unlike later adaptations, the *Ghaṭikāra Sutta* mentions no aspiration or vow to achieve Buddhahood, nor does Kassapa Buddha deliver a prediction of Jotipāla's future awakening; moreover, no extraordinary deeds are recorded of Jotipāla after ordination [Anālayo 2013; Chen 2015]. Instead, the narrative primarily celebrates the exemplary qualities and devotion of the potter Ghaṭikāra [Anālayo 2013; Chen 2015]. The Bodhisattva's initial lack of respect toward Kassapa Buddha presented an ethical difficulty for later traditions, becoming a celebrated conundrum addressed in the *Milindapañha* [SuttaCentral; Chen 2015].

Curated parallels include *Madhyama-āgama* 63 (MĀ 63), versions preserved in the *Mahāvastu* (titled *Jyotipāla Sūtra*), the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Bhaiṣajyavastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (where the Brahmin youth is named Uttara), Tibetan Kangyur D 1, and Taishō 197.10 [SuttaCentral; Gnoli 1977; Skilling, Eṣā agrā; Galasek 2016]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama*, and the Tibetan Vinayavastu [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, DharmaNexus records substantial textual reuse with the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* (DN 14), multiple Vinaya Khandhakas (notably Kd 1, Kd 6, Kd 8, and Kd 16), and the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.5.6) [DharmaNexus].
